title: 'Fast Tech' Cheap Gadgets Cause Costly E-Waste
paragraphs: The fashion industry has long been criticized for "fast fashion," cheap clothing that is quickly bought and thrown away. Now, environmental experts are warning about a similar problem in the world of electronics, which they call "fast tech."

Fast tech refers to cheap electrical and electronic items that people often buy on impulse and throw away quickly. Examples include earphones, charging cables, USB adapters, LED string lights, mini fans and single-use vapes. Many of these products contain lithium-ion batteries.

In 2026, the WEEE Forum, an international organization that represents groups responsible for collecting and recycling electronic waste, chose fast tech as the focus of International E-Waste Day, which took place on October 14. According to Pascal Leroy, the organization's director general, fast tech is the blind spot of the e-waste world.

A survey of more than 10,000 adults in 12 European countries, carried out for the WEEE Forum, found that 87% owned at least one fast tech product, and 78% had bought one during the previous year. However, 23% said they put unwanted fast tech items in their household rubbish. The problem is that people often do not think of these small items as electronic waste, so most of them are never properly collected or recycled. In the UK, a study by the organization Material Focus estimated that more than half a billion small fast tech electrical items were bought in 2023, which is about 16 every second.

Fast tech also creates serious safety risks. When devices containing batteries are thrown away with ordinary rubbish, the batteries can catch fire if they are crushed or punctured in garbage trucks or waste facilities. According to the WEEE Forum, 36% of e-waste operators reported a battery-related fire at their facility in the past year. In France, fires at waste treatment facilities linked to lithium batteries doubled between 2019 and 2023.

The WEEE Forum advises people to recognize that any small device with a plug, cable or battery should be treated as electronic waste. Such items should be taken to official collection points or stores that accept them. In the European Union, online retailers are legally required to accept small electronic items for free.
